titleStmt.title: Information Memorandum From the Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs (Abrams) to Secretary of State Shultz

div.head: 407. Information Memorandum From the Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs (Abrams) to Secretary of State Shultz

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: Paraguay: An Old Caudillo Faces the Future

div.p: SUMMARY: President Stroessner is struggling to contain opposition not only from frustrated sectors with increased political and economic expectations, but from within his own party, as well. He has resorted to his traditional method of applied political acumen, combined with selective repression, to contain this latest wave of opposition. END SUMMARY.
During the past few months, the GOP has taken the offensive against its moderate democratic opposition:
—An increasing number of noncommunist opposition leaders have been jailed on spurious charges of sedition;
—Labor leaders have been arrested and publicly beaten for attempting to organize, and peacefully demonstrate and strike.
—Private meetings of the democratic opposition have been violently disrupted.
—Rural workers involved in legitimate land disputes have been physically mistreated by local police authorities.

President Stroessner, 74, has consistently defeated previous surges of opposition activity with combination of repression and personal political acumen. Moreover, he has been able to count on the support of the military and the 100 year-old Colorado Party. The situation is evolving, however,
and today, the Colorado Party is suffering serious internecine conflict arising from disparate elements maneuvering for position in the “post-Stroessner” era. Deteriorating economic conditions are impacting adversely on the recently-expanded middle class, which previously looked to Stroessner to provide order and stability, but now is beginning to see him as an impediment to modernization.

The GOP thinks its visceral anti-communism should guarantee visible USG support and purports to be surprised when successive US Ambassadors do not deliver it. Ambassador Taylor’s contacts with the democratic opposition have incurred its wrath, as did our November 20 press statement calling on it to respect freedom of assembly and expression. The FRG in Bonn and the EC in Asuncion have made démarches, as we have done in Washington. Further, the GOP can no longer rely on the tacit approval of now-democratic Argentina and Brazil.

On the other hand, the GOP has benefited politically and financially from support from the Japanese Government. Paraguay, with a relatively large Japanese emigre community, is the largest Latin American recipient of bilateral Japanese aid. We have made the GOJ aware of our human rights concerns, but the GOJ has continued to devote a disproportionate amount of its assistance to Paraguay.

The opposition (both within and outside the Colorado Party) has identified the 1988 elections as a showdown, and can be expected to continue turning up the heat on Stroessner. We are not optimistic that increased internal and external pressure will cause Stroessner to moderate his policies, as he prepares for yet another term.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Bureau of Inter-American Affairs, Assistant Secretary Files, Special Collection—Iran Contra—Noriega, Lot 95D407, Chron (1987). Confidential. Drafted on December 15, 1986 by Bolton; cleared by Gelbard and Flower. Printed from an uninitialed copy.

In telegram 363989 to Asuncion, November 21, 1986 the Department forwarded the text of its November 21 press statement noting the detention of Paraguayan opposition leaders and urging the Paraguayan Government “to consider the release of these individuals as a demonstration of its respect for internationally accepted norms regarding freedom of assembly and speech.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D860890–0946)

In telegram 395249 to Asuncion, December 23, 1986 the Department noted that on December 18, Gelbard had given Martínez a démarche regarding Radio Nanduti and political repression in Paraguay. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D860975–0127)
